Level 2 · Intermediate · Week 9

Event-Driven Games

Keys and timers make things happen; a game loop moves the world one frame at a time.

What you will learn

  • How to make keys call your functions with onkey and listen.
  • How a game loop with ontimer moves everything one frame at a time.
  • How to keep the game’s state in a dictionary and check if two things are touching.
  • How to start planning your own final project.

The big idea: games wait for events

Most programs you wrote ran from top to bottom and stopped. A game waits. When something happens (a key press, a timer ringing), turtle calls one of your functions. The thing that happens is an event; the function that answers it is a handler.

Keys call handlers

def go_left():
    player.setx(player.xcor() - 20)

screen.onkey(go_left, "Left")   # when Left is pressed, call go_left
screen.listen()                 # switch on the "doorbell" for keys

Notice: go_left has no brackets in the onkey line. We hand turtle the function, and turtle calls it later. With brackets, Python would call it right away, only once.

The game loop

A game is like a flip book: every frame the world moves a tiny bit. Our game loop does one frame, then asks turtle to call it again soon.

One frame of Dodge the Meteors (shortened)

state = {"score": 0, "running": True}

def game_loop():
    for meteor in meteors:                      # a list of turtles
        meteor.sety(meteor.ycor() - 8)          # 1. move
        if is_touching(meteor.xcor(), meteor.ycor(),
                       player.xcor(), player.ycor(), 30):
            state["running"] = False            # 2. check: hit!
    if state["running"]:
        screen.ontimer(game_loop, 50)           # 4. again in 50 ms

Touching = close enough

Two things touch when the distance between them is small. math.dist measures the distance between two points: math.dist((0, 0), (30, 40)) gives 50.0. If that is less than about 30, the meteor hit the player.

Your final project starts now!

For the next three weeks you will build your own program, alone or with a partner. Read the Project Brief and choose:

Option A: Arcade Game Option B: Art Studio
A turtle game with keys, a timer and a score, like Dodge the Meteors or Star Catcher. The file saves high scores. A program that makes designs (often random) and can save and load them, like Dot Art from a File.

Both must use: functions that return values, a list, a dictionary, a loop or game loop, a file, and at least 3 tests. Milestone M1 (start of next week): Planning page 1 (pitch), page 2 (pseudocode or flowchart) and, in a pair, page 3 (task split).

TipBorrowing pictures or sounds

Pictures and sounds belong to the people who made them. Only use ones with an open license (CC0: free for anyone; CC BY: free if you give credit), ask a grown-up to help you find them, and write a credit in your code, like # Star sound by Mei (CC BY). Turtle’s own shapes are always fine!

New words

event
Something that happens while a program runs: a key press, a click, a timer ringing.
handler
The function that runs when an event happens.
listen()
Tells the turtle window to start hearing key presses.
game loop
A function that does one frame of the game, then sets a timer to run again.
frame
One tiny step of a game: everything moves a little, then it is drawn.
collision
Two things touching. We check it with the distance between them.
license / attribution
The rules for using someone’s work / giving them credit for it.

Homework: Event-Driven Games

15–20 minutes. Do both Core parts; Challenge and Creative are optional.

CorePart 1: Stamp Studio (about 10 minutes)

Folder: exercises/week09/hw-stamp-studio. An art program you play with the keyboard. The current shape and color are kept in a dictionary called studio.

  1. Open starter.py, press Run and click the window. Arrows move, s stamps. p and n do nothing yet.

  2. TODO 1: next_index(index, length) returns the next position and goes back to 0 after the last one. Fill in: next_index(2, 4) = (blank to fill in) next_index(3, 4) = (blank to fill in)

  3. TODO 2: write next_color(), a twin of next_shape().

  4. TODO 3: connect "p" and "n" with screen.onkey(...). No brackets after the function name!

CorePart 2: Project pitch, milestone M1 (about 8 minutes)

Take out your Project Brief. Fill in Planning page 1: My pitch. If you work with a partner, do it together (in person, or bring your ideas next week). Bring the Brief to the next session: we start by checking milestone M1.

ChallengePlan it, upgrade it

  • Start Planning page 2 of the Project Brief: write the pseudocode or draw the flowchart of your project’s main loop.

  • Or add a key to Stamp Studio that makes the stamps bigger and smaller with stamper.shapesize(...). Keep the size in the studio dictionary.

CreativeDraw your game screen

On paper, draw what your project will look like when it is running. Label every part: the player or brush, the things that move, the score or menu, and the keys. Use shapes and labels, not only colors, so everyone can tell the parts apart.
